# Portal fields

**Title** (146 of 500 characters)

SAMA: Skin-tone-equitable measurement of heart rate and heart-rate variability from facial video, towards camera-based care for Indian populations

**Project summary** (@@SUMMARY_CHARS@@ of 3,000 characters)

<!--SUMMARY-->
Video consultations now reach crores of Indians through eSanjeevani, yet no vital sign is measured from their cameras. Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) reads the pulse from tiny colour changes in facial skin with an ordinary webcam or phone, but the signal weakens in darker skin, dim light and compressed video: the same optical problem that made pulse oximeters miss low oxygen in darker-skinned patients. To our knowledge, no Indian dataset measures skin tone with an instrument, records ECG-grade ground truth and tests the compression that teleconsultations use. SAMA (Sanskrit: equal) will measure, explain, fix and guarantee camera-based heart rate (HR) and heart-rate variability (HRV) across Indian skin tones over 36 months. WP1 records 150 adults in three colorimeter-measured skin-tone strata (Individual Typology Angle), balanced for gender, with 1 kHz ECG, four synchronised cameras, two light levels and a seven-level compression ladder, during rest, a mock teleconsultation, film clips from the PI's Indian database (AFDI), mental stress and post-exercise recovery. WP2 audits 10 rPPG methods and splits each person's error into skin optics, light, device and compression. WP3 develops the SAMA method: skin-tone-adaptive exposure, calibrated noise-weighted pulse extraction, and a reliability gate that gives 90% intervals and withholds readings it cannot trust, with coverage and abstention audited per stratum. WP4 tests HRV agreement with ECG and releases an open toolkit and an Android research demonstrator. A November 2026 pilot on {{P:participants.n:d}} Indian volunteers ran the recording, synchronisation, compression and analysis pipeline end to end. Five hypotheses, to be pre-registered, each have one primary test whose power was simulated. Outputs: an open dataset, reference error tables for developers and regulators, open code and four papers. No clinical deployment is claimed.
<!--/SUMMARY-->

**Keywords:** remote photoplethysmography; skin tone; video compression; heart-rate variability; conformal prediction; digital health

**Objectives** (@@OBJECTIVES_CHARS@@ of 1,500 characters)

<!--OBJECTIVES-->
1. Build SAMA-150: 150 adults in three colorimeter-measured skin-tone strata, balanced for gender, with 1 kHz ECG, four synchronised cameras, two light levels and a seven-level video-compression ladder.
2. Quantify how the heart-rate and HRV error of 10 rPPG methods changes with skin tone, and split it into skin-optics, light, device and compression components, testing whether compression widens the skin-tone gap.
3. Develop the SAMA method (skin-tone-adaptive exposure, calibrated noise-weighted extraction, and a reliability gate with per-stratum audit) and test whether it lowers darker-stratum heart-rate error by a pre-registered margin without raising error elsewhere.
4. Test whether camera-derived HRV agrees with ECG across and within skin-tone strata, and release an open dataset, toolkit and on-device Android research demonstrator.
<!--/OBJECTIVES-->

**Expected output and outcome** (@@OUTCOME_CHARS@@ of 1,500 characters)

<!--OUTCOME-->
1. SAMA-150, to our knowledge the first Indian rPPG dataset with colorimeter-measured skin tone, 1 kHz ECG and a controlled compression ladder (faces under controlled access; signals and labels open).
2. Reference error tables by skin tone, light, device and bitrate for telehealth developers, standards bodies and regulators.
3. An open rPPG method that withholds readings it cannot trust, with coverage and abstention reported per stratum.
4. Evidence on whether camera-based HRV is valid enough for stress assessment in each skin-tone group.
5. Four papers (dataset descriptor, audit, method, HRV), open code, an Android research demonstrator and a developer workshop.
6. One trained research fellow (JRF to SRF), one project associate, and a reusable physiological-video recording facility at SVNIT.

# 1. Origin of the proposal

SAMA asks whether an ordinary phone or laptop camera can give every Indian, whatever their skin tone, a trustworthy heart rate and heart-rate variability (HRV), and it shows exactly where it cannot. The question grows out of the PI's own record:

- His M.Tech work measured heart rate from facial video in different user states (best paper, IHCI 2014).
- His PhD and postdoctoral work showed that cardiac and brain dynamics jointly predict emotional arousal in Indian viewers (Brain Sciences 2022), using the Affective Film Dataset from India (AFDI), which he built and validated (2023).
- His group validated a low-cost physiological recording device against a laboratory reference system (Frontiers in Neuroscience 2025).

Joining a Department of Artificial Intelligence turned this into a deployable question. Three facts make it urgent.

1. **Scale.** eSanjeevani, India's national telemedicine service, crossed 50 crore teleconsultations in October 2026. Each consultation has a camera, but no vital sign is measured from it.
2. **A known equity failure in optical sensing.** Optical sensors depend on how light passes through skin. Pulse oximeters missed hidden low oxygen almost three times as often in Black patients as in white patients (Sjoding et al. 2020). In camera sensing, a 54-person skin-tone-labelled study (VITAL) found that a standard facial-averaging pipeline's heart-rate error was 6.2 beats a minute for Fitzpatrick types V–VI against 3.9 for types I–II (Chari et al. 2020), and darker skin is under-represented in public rPPG datasets (Bondarenko et al. 2025).
3. **India is missing.** The two Indian rPPG datasets we found record heart rate against a finger oximeter in 44 adults (Dasari et al. 2021) and respiratory rate, with a finger-oximeter pulse channel, in 119 videos (Saikia et al. 2026). Neither measures skin tone with an instrument, uses ECG, or tests video compression.

**Scope.** SAMA is a measurement-science project in healthy adults. It produces the evidence and open tools that any later clinical validation or platform decision would need. It builds no medical device and claims no deployment.

![Figure 1. SAMA measures, explains, fixes and guarantees camera-based pulse measurement across Indian skin tones in four work packages, each ending in an output that stands on its own.](proposal/figures/Fig1_SAMA_overview_v2.png){width=100%}

# 2. Status of research and the gap

## 2.1 International status

**Methods.** Remote photoplethysmography recovers the pulse from colour changes in facial skin (Verkruysse et al. 2008). Signal-processing methods separate pulse from noise by blind source separation (Poh et al. 2010) or skin-reflectance models (CHROM, de Haan and Jeanne 2013; POS, Wang et al. 2017). Deep networks followed (DeepPhys, PhysNet, TS-CAN, PhysFormer, EfficientPhys). The open rPPG-Toolbox (Liu et al. 2023) benchmarks 11 methods on common footing. Its tables show the field's core weakness: trained networks reach about 1 beat a minute on clean laboratory video but 9–18 on the harder MMPD set (unsupervised methods: 12–22).

**Skin tone.** A meta-analysis found larger errors for darker skin (Nowara et al. 2020). On VITAL, a facial-averaging baseline's error rose from 3.9 to 6.2 beats a minute between Fitzpatrick types I–II and V–VI (Chari et al. 2020). Their optical analysis traced the bias to camera noise rather than biophysics: melanin leaves the pulse's relative size almost unchanged but lowers the light reaching the sensor. MMPD (Tang et al. 2023) reported errors above 10 beats a minute for most unsupervised methods on Fitzpatrick types IV–VI. The largest skin-tone analysis we found, of 893 participants from the Vital Videos dataset (Toye 2023; Tang et al. 2024), also labels skin tone by Fitzpatrick type. Skin tone is almost always labelled by eye, and annotators apply the Fitzpatrick scale inconsistently (Barrett et al. 2023).

**Compression.** Video compression degrades rPPG (McDuff et al. 2017), and networks have been built for compressed video (Yu et al. 2019). Whether compression widens the skin-tone gap has not been tested on recorded people. The only study we found is an unreviewed 2026 simulation (TRACE-rPPG): compression did not widen the gap in mean error, because darker skin was already near failure, while signal fidelity fell far more for darker skin.

**HRV.** HRV needs individual beats, which rPPG recovers less reliably. RMSSD from 60-second video correlated only r = 0.53 with a finger-PPG reference in 10 participants (Finžgar and Podržaj 2020). A 2026 pilot found r = 0.88 for lnRMSSD at rest against ECG, in 35 white participants, without an ICC (Pstras et al. 2026).

**Reliability.** Recent work estimates rPPG uncertainty with Bayesian networks (Ma and Chen 2025) or corrects implausible heart rates (Tian et al. 2026); neither reports reliability by skin tone. A 2026 metrology guide for PPG describes conformal prediction among uncertainty methods (Harris et al. 2026), and statistics offers intervals with equal coverage for every group (Romano et al. 2020). We found no rPPG study that audits reliability, coverage and abstention, by skin tone.

## 2.2 National status

Dasari et al. (2021) recorded 44 Indian adults indoors on a smartphone against a finger oximeter: heart rate only, no instrument-measured skin tone. Saikia, Gupta and colleagues (IIT Indore, 2026) released 119 videos for respiratory rate and showed that skin-tone-aware channel weighting helps, with weaker results at both ends of the skin-tone range for lack of samples. The PI's video heart-rate (2014) and cardiac–emotion (2022) studies are the closest Indian work on affective cardiac sensing. No Indian group, to our knowledge, has released an ECG-referenced, instrument-measured skin-tone rPPG dataset.

## 2.3 The gap, and what is new

| Closest prior work | What it did | What it left open |
|------------|----------------|----------------|
| Chari et al. 2020 (VITAL) | 54 people, Fitzpatrick labels, two lights; physics of skin-tone bias | PPG reference; no HRV; no controlled compression; no Indian participants |
| Tang et al. 2023 (MMPD) | 33 people, Fitzpatrick III–VI, phone video, four lights | Finger-PPG reference; already-compressed video; heart rate only |
| Tang et al. 2024 (Vital Videos data) | 893 people, Fitzpatrick labels | Visual labels; no ECG-grade HRV; no compression ladder |
| Dasari et al. 2021 | 44 Indian adults, smartphone | Oximeter reference; heart rate only; no measured skin tone |
| TRACE-rPPG 2026 | Compression × skin tone, simulated | No recorded people; not peer reviewed |
| Liu et al. 2023 (rPPG-Toolbox) | Common benchmark of 11 methods | Heart rate only; no results by skin tone |

SAMA adds five things, each new to our knowledge in combination:

1. **Skin tone measured with an instrument** (colorimeter ITA°), not judged by eye, in an Indian sample; with the camera's own ITA° estimate and Monk ratings validated against it.
2. **An error budget.** A lossless reference camera, synchronised consumer cameras, two light levels and an offline compression ladder let each person's error be split into skin optics, light, device and codec.
3. **The first real-data test of whether compression widens the skin-tone gap,** with two competing predictions set out in advance (Figure 2).
4. **Fairness at capture, not only in the algorithm:** skin-tone-adaptive exposure tested against auto-exposure on the same phone model.
5. **A reliability audit:** 90% intervals with the share of withheld readings and the interval coverage reported for every stratum, and HRV judged against 1 kHz ECG.

The individual tools (POS, group-DRO, FiLM conditioning, conformal prediction) are established; what is new is their use with measured skin tone, a controlled compression ladder and ECG ground truth, and the per-stratum audit. Whether each step helps is tested by ablation, not assumed.

![Figure 2. Each stage from room light to video codec can shrink the pulse or bury it in noise; darker skin is affected at the epidermis, the sensor and the codec. The two predictions for compression are tested in H2.](proposal/figures/Fig2_mechanism.png){width=96%}

# 3. Research questions and pre-registered hypotheses

SAMA answers four questions:

1. How large is the skin-tone gradient in camera heart-rate and HRV error among Indians, and how much of it comes from light, device and compression?
2. Does video compression widen that gradient, or does darker-skin error already sit at a floor?
3. Can changes at capture and in the algorithm reduce the gap, while keeping reliability auditable in every skin-tone group?
4. Is camera-derived HRV valid enough for stress assessment in each skin-tone group?

Each hypothesis has one primary endpoint, one test and a numeric success criterion, registered on the Open Science Framework before the first participant is recorded. Skin-tone strata are fixed in advance from Individual Typology Angle categories (Del Bino and Bernerd 2013): lighter, ITA° above 28; middle, 10 to 28; darker, 10 or below. The primary baseline for H1 to H3 is POS, chosen in advance as the best-performing unsupervised method on two of the three rPPG-Toolbox test sets in our reading of its tables. Error is the absolute heart-rate error against ECG in 30-second windows, averaged per participant. The decision rule of every criterion below was simulated under the assumptions of section 6.

| Hypothesis | Primary endpoint | Test | Success criterion | Power at 45 analysable per stratum |
|--------|------------|--------|----------------|--------|
| **H1** Error rises as skin tone darkens | Log of per-participant heart-rate MAE; POS; lossless reference video; both lights | Slope on ITA° (continuous), one-sided | Slope below zero at p < 0.05. Estimand: ratio of errors per 10° of ITA°. Sensitivity: rank correlation; raw MAE | 0.83 |
| **H2** Compression changes the skin-tone gap | Compression penalty: MAE at 500 kbps H.264 minus lossless MAE | Slope of penalty on ITA°, two-sided, 95% CI | Slope below zero (p < 0.05) supports prediction A (widening). A 90% CI inside ±1.0 bpm per 75° of ITA° (equivalence; the same smallest effect as A) supports B. Otherwise inconclusive | 0.89 for A; 0.86 for B if no widening |
| **H3** Adaptive exposure helps darker skin | Phone B (adaptive) minus phone A (auto-exposure) MAE, darker stratum, standard light (where extra exposure can add photons) | Paired test, one-sided | Mean reduction at p < 0.05; 1.0 bpm is the smallest reduction that matters. Dim light and lights pooled are secondary | 0.96 (0.50 if the true gain is 0.5) |
| **H4** The SAMA method lowers darker-stratum error | Darker-stratum MAE over **all** windows, SAMA vs best baseline, held-out participants | Paired, one-sided, 95% lower bound | Lower 95% bound of the relative reduction at least 10% (target reduction 30%) | 0.92 |
| **H5** Camera HRV agrees with ECG | Resting ln RMSSD from the SAMA method, lossless video, standard light | ICC(2,1), absolute agreement; strata pooled | Lower 95% bound at least 0.60. Each stratum's ICC (with a darker-stratum bound of 0.50 as a pre-registered secondary), Bland–Altman limits and the best baseline are reported | > 0.99 at true ICC 0.85; 0.92 at 0.75 |
| **E1** (exploratory) Stress and arousal are as detectable from camera as from ECG | Leave-one-subject-out accuracy, camera vs ECG features | Paired comparison per stratum | Reported with confidence intervals; no confirmatory claim | n/a |

**Pre-registered secondary outcomes of H4** (reported with participant-bootstrap CIs, not success criteria): lighter-stratum MAE not raised by more than 10%; coverage of the 90% intervals per stratum, against a non-inferiority margin of 85%; best-to-worst stratum gap; abstention rate and useful yield (readings shown and within ±5 bpm) per stratum. Error is scored on all windows, with withheld windows scored at their point estimate, because error on shown windows falls mechanically as more windows are withheld. **H5 secondary:** RMSSD reactivity (mental arithmetic minus rest) and per-stratum lower bounds.

*Why these criteria and not simpler ones.* Each alternative was simulated and rejected. Read as a point estimate, "at least 30% lower" is met only half the time when the true reduction is exactly 30% (power 0.50); requiring five H4 criteria together failed in every simulated study of the design rehearsal; and requiring an ICC point estimate of 0.75 succeeds only half the time when the true ICC is 0.75. The H5 anchor (r = 0.88) is camera-versus-ECG agreement of resting level, so the primary H5 endpoint is resting level and reactivity is secondary. H3 is tested in standard light because at 100 lux the 1/30 s exposure cap leaves only sensor gain, which adds no photons; pooling the lights would dilute the expected effect.

*Multiplicity.* The five hypotheses answer separate questions, each the primary claim of a separate paper, and no single conclusion is drawn from them jointly; each is tested at α = 0.05. Holm-adjusted p-values across H1–H5 are reported alongside.

**Every outcome is publishable.** If H1 fails, Indian users face a smaller gap than feared, and SAMA-150 shows it. If H2 supports A, low-bandwidth calls are a hidden equity risk and measuring on the phone before compression is the remedy; if B, the remedy must come at capture and in the algorithm; if inconclusive, the error tables still bound the effect. If H3 or H4 fail, the error budget still shows developers and regulators exactly where camera vital signs must not be shown.

<div class="pb"></div>

# 4. Methodology

Four work packages run as measure, explain, fix and validate (Figure 3) over 36 months. Recording ends at month 16, so analysis, method development and release have twenty months on complete data. Each package ends in a deliverable that stands on its own.

![Figure 3. Work packages, their tasks, hypotheses and deliverables over 36 months.](proposal/figures/Fig3_work_packages_36m.png){width=100%}

## WP1 · SAMA-150 dataset (months 1–20)

**Participants.** 150 adults aged 18–60: SVNIT students and staff, who come from across India, and Surat residents. Recruitment is by quota: 50 per skin-tone stratum, 25 women and 25 men in each, so that 45 per stratum remain analysable after a 10% loss. Skin tone is measured at screening, so each quota fills by measurement, not by guess. At least 30 participants will be aged 35 or over, to widen the HRV range. Ten protocol-pilot sessions in months 3–4 test the full rig (ECG, colorimeter, four cameras) and are separate from the 150 and from the November 2026 feasibility pilot (section 5). Indian colorimeter data suggest the **lighter** stratum is the scarce one (about 15% of adults have cheek ITA° above 28; Pawar et al. 2024), so screening of about 330–390 volunteers is planned (section 9.3).

**Who is excluded, and why.** Exclusions are limited to conditions that make the ECG ground truth invalid.

| Condition | Rule | Reason |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| Pacemaker or other implanted cardiac device | Excluded | A paced rhythm makes HRV non-physiological |
| Known atrial fibrillation or other sustained arrhythmia | Excluded | RMSSD and SDNN are defined only on normal beats (Task Force 1996) |
| Occasional ectopic beats | Kept | Ectopic beats found on ECG are edited; windows with more than 5% edited beats are dropped from HRV analysis only |
| Beta-blockers or other heart-rate-lowering medicines | Kept and recorded | Left out of H5 and E1 only; heart-rate accuracy is unaffected |
| Beard, spectacles, bindi, make-up, head covering | Kept and recorded | Common among Indian users and they affect rPPG, so they belong in the data |
| Any "yes" on the PAR-Q+ questionnaire | Kept; step test skipped | Safety |

**Skin tone, measured three ways.** (i) *Reference:* a portable colorimeter takes three CIELAB readings each at the forehead and both cheeks; the Individual Typology Angle (Chardon et al. 1991) is computed from their mean, ITA° = arctan((L* − 50)/b*) × 180/π. (ii) *Camera:* the same ITA° is computed from each camera after colour-chart calibration (and, as in the pilot, against a grey card), so the project can report how well a camera alone estimates skin tone; a video-to-ITA° model is trained on the colorimeter labels and evaluated by cross-validation. (iii) *Visual:* two trained raters give independent Monk Skin Tone ratings and participants rate themselves and report their Fitzpatrick type; inter-rater agreement (weighted kappa, ICC) is reported. Strata are always assigned from the colorimeter.

**Recording set-up.** All streams share one clock (Lab Streaming Layer) and an LED flash at the start and end of every block; in addition, camera and reference pulses are aligned by cross-correlation, which the pilot used to measure how stable the alignment is between windows (the constant delay between face and finger pulse is absorbed by the alignment and is not counted as error). A month-3 test checks that drift stays below one reference-video frame (17 ms).

| Stream | Device | Why it is there |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| Reference video | USB3 machine-vision colour camera, 60 fps, raw Bayer of an 800 × 800 face region, saved losslessly (FFV1) | Best-case signal, and the source of the compression ladder |
| Webcam | USB 3 webcam, 1280 × 720 at 30 fps in uncompressed YUYV (the pilot used 640 × 480); the pixel format is logged per session | Laptop consultation |
| Phone A | Mid-range Android phone, front camera, Open Camera with automatic exposure | A typical patient phone |
| Phone B | Same phone model, Open Camera with exposure set by the skin-tone-adaptive rule (WP3) | Tests H3; the two units swap roles between participants |
| Live call | Webcam stream through a self-hosted Jitsi Meet server, capped at 500 kbps, recorded at the receiving end | Checks that offline compression predicts a real call |
| ECG | BITalino, lead II, 1,000 Hz | Ground truth for beats and HRV |
| Chest-strap ECG | Polar H10, RR intervals | Second reference and backup |
| Finger PPG | Fingertip pulse oximeter with PC logging | Comparability with public datasets and the pilot |
| Skin conductance, respiration | BITalino EDA and respiration belt | Arousal check; breathing, which shapes HRV |
| Light | Lux meter at the face; colour chart and grey card in the first frame of every block | Covariate and colour calibration |

**Session protocol** (Figure 4). About 80 minutes, of which 47 are recorded on every stream at once. Each half of the session repeats the same blocks under one light level, about 500 lux diffuse LED or about 100 lux overhead light, so every condition is measured within the same person under both. Light order, the assignment of the four AFDI clips (two neutral, two high-arousal) and which phone unit is adaptive are counterbalanced. In the mock teleconsultation, a researcher on a video link asks ten scripted history-taking questions and the participant answers naturally. A one-minute step test followed by three seated minutes gives each person a falling heart rate across the range seen with fever or anxiety. Participants are paid ₹750.

![Figure 4. One session. The inner timeline is to scale.](proposal/figures/Fig3_session_protocol.png){width=92%}

**Compression ladder.** The lossless reference video is resized to 720p at 30 fps and re-encoded with ffmpeg: H.264 at 2,000, 1,000, 500 and 250 kbps (two-pass, constant bitrate, as in a call), and VP8 (the codec WebRTC calls must support) at 500 and 250 kbps. With the lossless original this gives seven levels per recording, all measured on identical face regions. The scripts are released and were exercised in the pilot.

**Quality control.** An automatic check runs after every session (frame rate and gaps, face present, light, reference coverage, synchronisation); the same code produced the pilot's usable-session count. A session is re-recorded if more than 20% of its ECG is unusable. Monthly review of quota progress.

**Data handling.** Faces cannot be anonymised, so consent is tiered: SVNIT research use only, or sharing under a data-use agreement. Raw video is kept encrypted on an offline server and released only to signed institutional users. ECG, derived signals, ITA° values and labels are released openly under CC BY 4.0. Notice, consent, purpose limitation and retention follow the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and its 2025 Rules.

**Deliverables.** D1.1 pre-registered protocol, ethics approval and synchronisation test, month 3. D1.2 first 75 participants, month 10. D1.3 all 150 participants and quality report, month 16. D1 data release and dataset descriptor submitted to *Scientific Data*, month 20.

## WP2 · Bias audit and error budget (months 8–22)

**Baselines.** Ten methods: six unsupervised (Green, ICA, CHROM, POS, LGI, PBV) and four neural (DeepPhys, TS-CAN, PhysNet, EfficientPhys) in rPPG-Toolbox. TS-CAN and EfficientPhys are included because they run on phones. Each neural model is tested as released (pretrained on PURE, UBFC-rPPG or SCAMPS) and fine-tuned on SAMA-150 by five-fold cross-validation split by participant, with every stratum in every fold. The six unsupervised methods are already implemented in the SAMA toolkit and checked against the rPPG-Toolbox code.

**Metrics.** In 30-second windows overlapping by 15 seconds: heart-rate MAE, RMSE, Pearson r, signal-to-noise ratio, and the share of windows within the heart-rate-monitor tolerance of ±5 beats a minute or ±10%, whichever is greater (ANSI/AAMI EC13:2002); in 60-second windows, inter-beat-interval error and RMSSD and SDNN error; fairness: worst-stratum MAE and the gap and ratio between worst and best strata.

**Error budget.** For participant *i*, block *b* and each combination of light ℓ, device *d* and codec *c*, a linear mixed model splits the error into parts:

log(1 + e~ibℓdc~) = β~0~ + β~1~ ITA~i~ + Σ~k~ γ~k~ X~k~ + Σ~k~ δ~k~ ITA~i~ X~k~ + θ′z~ib~ + u~i~ + v~b~ + ε

Here *e* is the window's absolute heart-rate error; X~k~ are indicators for dim light, each consumer device and each codec level, so γ~k~ is a component's average cost and δ~k~ how that cost changes with skin tone; *z* holds head motion (from the face region), age, sex, beard and spectacles; u~i~ and v~b~ are random effects for participant and block type. Each stratum's budget (predicted error on lossless video in good light plus the increment from each component) is shown as a stacked bar with participant-bootstrap confidence intervals.

**H1 analysis.** The primary test regresses the log of each participant's mean MAE (POS, lossless reference video, both lights, seated blocks) on ITA°, one-sided; the reported effect is the ratio of errors per 10° of ITA°. Sensitivity: Spearman correlation, raw MAE, the mixed model. Secondary analyses repeat this for the other nine methods with Holm correction, and replace ITA° with Monk and Fitzpatrick ratings to show what visual labels miss.

**H2 analysis.** Each participant's penalty (MAE at 500 kbps H.264 minus lossless MAE) is regressed on ITA°, two-sided, with the three-way decision rule of section 3. Secondary analyses treat the ladder as a dose–response (ITA° × log bitrate), repeat it for VP8 and for signal-to-noise ratio, and compare live-call recordings with offline 500 kbps encoding.

**Deliverables.** D2.1 internal interim audit of the first 45 participants and power re-check, month 10. D2 audit paper and open reference error tables, month 22.

## WP3 · The SAMA method (months 10–30)

Chari et al. (2020) traced the skin-tone gap to too little pulse signal above camera noise. SAMA attacks that cause at three points: at capture, during extraction, and when deciding whether to report a number (Figure 5). Steps 3–6 are implemented in the open toolkit used in the pilot, each with a configuration switch for the ablations; steps 1 and 2 have been prototyped in simulation and are built on the study phones and cameras in WP3.

![Figure 5. The SAMA method. Steps 1, 4 and 6 combine established tools in a way not tested before with measured skin tone; steps 2, 3 and 5 adapt established methods. Whether each step helps is decided by ablation.](proposal/figures/Fig5_SAMA_method_v2.png){width=100%}

**Step 1. Skin-tone-adaptive exposure.** Phone auto-exposure is tuned for a pleasing picture, not for the pulse, and can leave a darker face low in the sensor's range, where noise and 8-bit rounding swamp the pulse. Before each block, a 10-second calibration measures the face's mean brightness. Exposure time (capped at 1/30 s to keep 30 frames a second) and then sensor gain are raised until the face reaches a target share of full scale with under 1% of skin pixels clipped. White balance is locked from the colour chart. The target is fixed from the protocol pilot. At 100 lux the exposure cap leaves only gain, which adds no photons, so the gain from this step is expected mainly in good light; H3 pools both lights and reports each.

**Step 2. Calibration and a measured noise model.** The 24-patch chart gives each camera's mapping to linear RGB. Static frames of the chart give the camera's noise variance at every brightness level (the photon-transfer method), so the expected noise of each skin patch is known rather than guessed.

**Step 3. Noise-weighted skin patches.** About 30 patches on the forehead and cheeks; eyes, mouth, beard, bindi and specular highlights are masked. Each patch is weighted by its pulse-band power divided by its expected noise variance, extending the signal-to-noise weighting of Chari et al. (2020) with a measured, camera-specific noise model.

**Step 4. Physics-guided extraction with worst-group training.** POS projection of the weighted linear RGB gives a candidate pulse. A small one-dimensional convolutional network (under 0.5 million parameters, so it runs on a phone; the current implementation has about 10,000) refines it from the patch traces. Feature-wise linear modulation (Perez et al. 2018) lets the network use the measured ITA° and face brightness. The loss combines negative Pearson correlation with a spectral heart-rate term. Training uses group distributionally robust optimisation (Sagawa et al. 2020) over six groups (three strata × two lights). Because SAMA-150 records ECG rather than contact PPG, the waveform target is a pulse template placed on the ECG R-peaks; public datasets supply contact-PPG targets for pre-training. Whether conditioning and worst-group training help is tested by ablation.

**Step 5. Sub-frame beat timing.** After band-pass filtering (0.7–3.0 Hz), pulse peaks are located by parabolic interpolation to 1 ms. Inter-beat intervals pass the same artefact rules as the ECG, then give heart rate, RMSSD and SDNN.

**Step 6. Reliability gate.** Split conformal prediction with normalised scores (Vovk et al. 2005; Romano et al. 2020) gives each window a 90% interval for heart rate:

s~j~ = |ĥ~j~ − h~j~| / σ̂(x~j~);  q̂~g~ = the ⌈0.9 (n~g~ + 1)⌉-th smallest s~j~ in group g;  C(x) = ĥ ± q̂~g~ σ̂(x)

Here ĥ is the camera estimate, h the ECG value, and σ̂(x) a difficulty score learned from patch signal-to-noise, motion and brightness. A reading is shown only if the half-width is at most 5 beats a minute; otherwise the system says "no reliable reading". Because windows from one person are correlated, calibration draws one window per participant and repeats the draw 200 times. Inside nested cross-validation, the gate is calibrated with **cross-conformal scores**: every outer-training participant is scored by a model that did not see them (Vovk 2015; Barber et al. 2021). A plain split would leave about seven calibration participants per stratum, too few for any finite 90% interval (nine are needed). Cross-conformal methods guarantee coverage of at least 1 − 2α (80%) in the worst case and are close to 90% in practice; coverage is therefore checked fold by fold, with quantiles from the other folds only. The primary gate is pooled across strata and fixed in advance; a per-stratum (Mondrian) gate is a pre-registered sensitivity analysis. The deployed gate is calibrated on the codec and device mix of deployment. Reported per stratum: coverage, interval width, abstention and useful yield.

**Training and validation.** Pre-training on public datasets (PURE, UBFC-rPPG, UBFC-Phys, SCAMPS); fine-tuning on SAMA-150 by nested cross-validation split by participant (five outer folds for testing, inner folds for settings). Ablations remove each step in turn. External tests on UBFC-Phys and MMPD. The best baseline for H4 is fixed as the baseline with the lowest darker-stratum MAE in the same outer folds.

**Measure before you compress.** Steps 2–6 also run on the compressed ladder, so the project reports, per stratum, how much accuracy is kept by measuring on the phone before video is compressed for the call.

**Deliverables.** D3 method paper, open model and code, month 30.

## WP4 · HRV, stress and release (months 18–36)

**HRV agreement (H5).** For every segment of at least 60 seconds, RMSSD and SDNN are computed from ECG and from the camera, with SAMA (primary) and the best baseline (secondary), using the same beat-editing rules for camera and ECG. The primary endpoint is resting ln RMSSD on lossless reference video in good light, judged by the lower 95% bound of ICC(2,1) with absolute agreement over all participants, interpreted with the bands of Koo and Li (2016); each stratum's ICC and Bland–Altman limits are reported, with a darker-stratum lower bound of 0.50 as a pre-registered secondary so that a pooled pass cannot hide a failure in darker skin. Secondary: RMSSD reactivity (mental arithmetic minus the preceding rest), the other lights, devices and codec levels; the paced-breathing block tests beat recovery when HRV is large; the respiration belt shows whether apparent HRV changes are driven by breathing.

**Stress and arousal (E1, exploratory).** Leave-one-subject-out classifiers (logistic regression and gradient boosting on heart rate, RMSSD, SDNN and pulse amplitude) separate arithmetic from rest and high- from low-arousal clips, trained once on ECG features and once on camera features; accuracy is compared per stratum with bootstrap intervals. Skin conductance gives an independent arousal check. This links SAMA to tele-mental-health (Tele-MANAS) without a confirmatory claim.

**On-device research demonstrator.** The SAMA model is exported (ONNX/TensorFlow Lite) and runs steps 1–6 inside an Android app built on Open Camera's exposure control, so no video leaves the phone. It is tested for latency, battery use and abstention on the two study phones and one entry-level phone, with recorded sessions and short live sessions with 10 lab volunteers under the same ethics approval. A desktop version (live heart rate, HRV, beat display and motion warnings) already exists and was used in the pilot. It is a research demonstrator: not a medical device and not for diagnosis.

**Release.** Toolkit v1.0 with model weights, reference error tables, codec scripts and the demonstrator's source code, on GitHub under an open licence. The dataset goes through a controlled-access portal, and SVNIT will offer it for listing on IndiaAI's AIKosh under the same terms. A one-day workshop at SVNIT shows telehealth developers how to use the tables and toolkit.

**Deliverables.** D4.1 HRV paper, month 32. D4.2 developer workshop, month 34. D4.3 toolkit v1.0, demonstrator and final report, month 36.

# 5. Preliminary work and pilot results

## 5.1 Already in hand

The PI has extracted heart rate from facial video (2014), built and validated the AFDI clips used here (2023), shown that cardiac signals track emotional arousal in Indian viewers (2022), and validated a low-cost physiological device against a reference system (2025). SVNIT provides laboratory space and a GPU cluster.

**An open, tested software pipeline.** For this proposal the team built the SAMA toolkit: the six unsupervised baselines (checked against the rPPG-Toolbox code), the SAMA steps 3–6 with configuration switches for every ablation, the compression ladder, synchronisation by cross-correlation, camera ITA° estimation against a grey card or colour chart, a video-to-skin-tone model, Monk-rating agreement statistics, a lab recorder that writes lossless video while showing live heart rate, HRV, beat timing and motion warnings, and the analysis that produced section 5.2. It has an automated test suite. Before any real recording, a full simulated rehearsal of the study (the design rehearsal) was used to check the design; its findings are the reason for the criteria chosen in sections 3 and 6 (simulation evidence about the design, not about people).

**Public data.** SAMA was trained only on public datasets with contact-PPG references ({{T:n_recordings:d}} recordings, {{T:n_participants:d}} participants of {{T:trained_on:list}}). In participant-level cross-validation its heart-rate error was {{T:cv.all.mae_sama:.2f}} beats a minute against {{T:cv.all.mae_pos:.2f}} for POS on the same windows; the gate withheld {{T:cv.all.abstention:pct}} of windows and its shown 90% intervals covered the reference in {{T:cv.all.coverage_shown:pct}}. Public datasets have no instrument skin-tone labels, so this model was trained skin-tone blind.

## 5.2 Pilot study on Indian volunteers (November 2026)

**Design.** {{P:participants.n:d}} volunteers (SVNIT students and staff; Monk Skin Tone {{P:participants.monk_min:g}} to {{P:participants.monk_max:g}}; camera-estimated ITA° {{P:participants.ita_min:.0f}}° to {{P:participants.ita_max:.0f}}°) were recorded with a webcam saved losslessly against a fingertip pulse oximeter (contact PPG) under two light levels, during rest, a mock consultation and mental arithmetic, following the SAMA protocol in miniature. The webcam video was re-encoded at 2,000, 1,000, 500 and 250 kbps (H.264) and 500 and 250 kbps (VP8). No colorimeter was available before funding: skin tone was estimated from the video against a grey card beside the cheek, and rated on the Monk scale by {{P:raters.rater_text}} ({{P:participants.strata_note}}). The SAMA model was trained on {{P:sama.trained_on_text}} only, so every pilot participant is an untouched test case. Windows in which a method produced no estimate were counted as failures, not dropped. Approval: SVNIT IEC [TO FILL: reference and date].

**Four results matter for this proposal:**

1. **Feasibility.** The camera-to-reference alignment varied by {{P:feasibility.sync_spread_ms_median:.0f}} ms between 30-second windows (robust SD, median over sessions); a session took {{P:feasibility.session_minutes_median:.0f}} minutes; {{P:feasibility.n_usable:d}} of {{P:feasibility.n_recorded:d}} recordings passed the automatic quality check.
2. **Skin tone.** Per 10° fall in camera ITA°, POS heart-rate error changed by a factor of {{P:skin_tone.POS.ratio_per_10deg_fall:.2f}} (95% CI {{P:skin_tone.POS.ratio_lo95:.2f}} to {{P:skin_tone.POS.ratio_hi95:.2f}}), that is by {{P:skin_tone.POS.rise_per_10deg_fall:+.2f}} beats a minute (Figure 6A). Camera ITA° and the Monk rating correlated with Spearman ρ = {{P:ita_vs_monk.spearman_rho:.2f}} (95% CI {{P:ita_vs_monk.lo95:.2f}} to {{P:ita_vs_monk.hi95:.2f}}; a negative value means camera ITA° fell as the Monk shade darkened).
3. **Compression.** At 500 kbps H.264, POS error changed by {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.darker.penalty:+.2f}} beats a minute in the darker group (n = {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.darker.n:d}}; 95% CI {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.darker.lo95:+.2f}} to {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.darker.hi95:+.2f}}) and by {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.lighter.penalty:+.2f}} in the lighter group (n = {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.lighter.n:d}}; 95% CI {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.lighter.lo95:+.2f}} to {{P:compression.POS.h264.by_stratum.lighter.hi95:+.2f}}) (Figure 6B).
4. **Agreement.** Camera minus reference heart rate (POS, lossless): bias {{P:agreement.POS.bias:+.2f}}, 95% limits {{P:agreement.POS.loa_lo:+.1f}} to {{P:agreement.POS.loa_hi:+.1f}} beats a minute, widened for repeated windows per person (Figure 6C).

**The SAMA method on Indian faces.** Trained on {{P:sama.trained_on_text}} only, SAMA's error on the pilot was {{P:sama.lossless.all.mae_sama_all:.2f}} beats a minute against {{P:sama.lossless.all.mae_primary_all:.2f}} for POS on the same windows; its gate withheld {{P:sama.lossless.all.abstention:pct}} of windows, and the shown 90% intervals covered the reference in {{P:sama.lossless.all.coverage_shown:pct}}.

![Figure 6. Pilot results. (A) Per-participant heart-rate error against ITA° for each method. (B) Error by bitrate in each skin-tone group. (C) Bland–Altman agreement with the reference. Produced by the released analysis from the pilot recordings.](@@FIG6@@){width=100%}

**What the pilot does and does not show.** These are feasibility numbers from a small sample, not tests of the hypotheses: every interval is wide, skin tone was estimated rather than measured, and the reference was a finger PPG rather than ECG. They show whether the set-up, synchronisation, compression ladder, skin-tone pipeline, reliability gate and analysis work end to end on Indian volunteers, and they give the between-person spread used to re-check the power analysis (section 6); the pilot's spread pools both lights and all blocks against a finger reference, so it is likely larger than SAMA-150's. Preparing the pilot also shaped the main protocol: a grey card replaces a white one (a white card can saturate when auto-exposure brightens a darker face), a 30-second motion check tunes the motion warning, and session quality control is automatic.

# 6. Sample size and statistics

With 50 participants recruited per stratum and 45 analysable after a 10% loss allowance, every confirmatory criterion of section 3 has power of 0.83 or more under the assumptions below (Figure 7). Forty per stratum (36 analysable) would give only 0.74 for H1 once its effect is anchored conservatively, which is why 50 are recruited. Power was estimated by simulating 2,000 studies per sample size, each assumption anchored in published data or set at the smallest effect that would change advice. The simulation code is released with the protocol (`analysis/proposal_power.py`, sharing its H1 model with the pilot's re-check). The selection of the best baseline for H4 is not modelled; it can only make H4 harder.

| Hypothesis | Assumed effect | Where it comes from | Spread assumed | Power at 36 / 45 / 50 analysable per stratum |
|--------|------------|------------|--------|------------|
| H1 | MAE rises by a factor of 1.57 from ITA° 50 to −25 (2.87 → 4.5 bpm) | Chari et al. (2020): 3.94 → 6.20 bpm between Fitzpatrick I–II and V–VI, a span of at least 75° of ITA° | Log-normal between-person spread (CV 0.6) | 0.74 / 0.83 / 0.86 (0.57 / 0.64 / 0.70 if CV 0.8; 0.90 / 0.95 / 0.97 if the full Fitzpatrick-range effect applied) |
| H2 | The 500 kbps penalty is 1.0 bpm larger at the darkest ITA° | Smallest difference that would change advice | Between-participant SD of penalty 1.0 | A: 0.81 / 0.89 / 0.91. B (±1.0 equivalence) if there is no widening: 0.75 / 0.86 / 0.92. Slope CI half-width 0.62 bpm per 75° at 45 |
| H3 | Adaptive exposure lowers darker-stratum MAE in standard light by 1.0 bpm | Smallest reduction that matters | SD of paired differences 2.0 (re-estimated at month 10) | 0.90 / 0.96 / 0.97 (0.45 / 0.50 / 0.54 at 0.5 bpm) |
| H4 | SAMA lowers darker-stratum MAE by 30% (4.5 → 3.15) | The target itself | SD of paired differences 2.0 (re-estimated at month 10) | 0.85 / 0.92 / 0.93 |
| H5 | True ICC 0.85 | Resting lnRMSSD r = 0.88 against ECG (Pstras et al. 2026; 35 white participants, so a weak anchor) | McGraw–Wong interval | > 0.99 / > 0.99 / > 0.99; at a true ICC of 0.75: 0.80 / 0.92 / 0.92; at 0.70: 0.43 / 0.50 / 0.52 |

![Figure 7. Power of each confirmatory criterion as worded, against analysable participants per stratum (2,000 simulated studies per point, α = 0.05).](proposal/figures/Fig7_power_revised.png){width=100%}

**What the simulations warned us about.** Type-I error of the H1 log-MAE test is 0.053 at the nominal 0.05. H1's power depends on the effect and on the spread, neither yet measured in Indian participants; the month-10 audit re-checks both. With a tighter equivalence margin of ±0.5 bpm per 75°, H2 could almost never establish "no widening" (probability 0.002); the margin is therefore the smallest effect of interest, which makes outcome B reachable (0.86) while an inconclusive result is still named. A reliability gate calibrated inside five-fold cross-validation by a plain split cannot give finite 90% intervals; cross-conformal calibration fixes this, and the pooled gate's coverage in a stratum reaches the 85% non-inferiority margin with probability 0.96. H3 has low power if the true gain is half the minimum important difference, and H5 if the true ICC is near 0.70; both are reported with their confidence intervals either way.

**Pilot re-check.** In the pilot, the between-person spread of log POS error around its skin-tone trend was {{P:power_recheck.H1.pilot_log_sd:.2f}} (assumed 0.55; 95% CI {{P:power_recheck.H1.sd_ci95.0:.2f}}–{{P:power_recheck.H1.sd_ci95.1:.2f}}). With the same model as above, that gives H1 power {{P:power_recheck.H1.power_45_at_pilot_sd:.2f}} at 45 per stratum, and {{P:power_recheck.H1.power_45_at_upper_sd:.2f}} at the upper confidence bound. {{P:power_recheck.H1.verdict}} The pilot's spread pools both lights and all blocks against a finger reference, so it overstates SAMA-150's; the month-10 audit repeats the check on 45 SAMA-150 participants with ECG.

**Analysis rules, fixed in advance.**

- *Multiplicity.* Each hypothesis has one primary test at α = 0.05, one-sided where the direction is stated. Secondary analyses within a hypothesis use Holm correction. Exploratory analyses are labelled as such.
- *Missing data.* Windows with unusable ECG are dropped by a pre-set quality rule. Participants with partial data stay in every analysis their data allow. The 10% allowance covers lost sessions.
- *Selective prediction.* Accuracy comparisons use all windows; error on shown windows is reported only next to the abstention rate.
- *Failures.* A window in which a method gives no estimate is a failure, scored against the participant's median estimate, and failure rates are reported per stratum, because dropping failures would favour the methods and skin tones that fail most.
- *Safeguard on the assumptions.* If the protocol pilot or the month-10 audit shows more spread than assumed, the power analysis is re-run and recruitment raised to up to 55 per stratum; the 15 extra sessions are budgeted (section 8).
- *Transparency.* Pre-registration on OSF before the first participant; deviations reported with reasons; analysis code released with every configuration file.

**Justification.**

- *ECG at 1,000 Hz* is needed because HRV ground truth depends on beat timing to the millisecond. Two BITalino kits mean one is always available: a failed or charging kit never cancels a booked session, and the spare runs the protocol pilot while the main rig is being set up. The Polar H10 sensors are a validated second reference and a backup. The fingertip oximeters keep the pilot's reference in the main study, so pilot and SAMA-150 results can be compared directly, and match the references of public datasets.
- *Four cameras are the experiment.* The machine-vision camera gives the best-case signal and the lossless source for the compression ladder; the webcams and phones give what patients use. Two units of one phone model isolate the effect of exposure (H3); the entry-level phone tests the demonstrator on a budget device.
- *The colorimeter* measures skin tone with an instrument, the basis of every skin-tone claim; it also provides the labels on which the camera's own skin-tone estimate is validated.
- *Controlled light* is needed to test light as a cause; the lux meter makes it a measured covariate.
- *Storage.* The reference camera records an 800 × 800 face region at 60 fps as raw Bayer, about 1.3 GB a minute after lossless compression; the webcam at 720p about 0.8 GB a minute. Over 175 sessions with 47 recorded minutes this is about 18–20 TB, held on two primary drives and mirrored to two encrypted offline backups. Raw faces never go to a cloud. Software is open source (rPPG-Toolbox, Open Camera, Jitsi Meet, ffmpeg, Lab Streaming Layer, the SAMA toolkit); model training uses SVNIT's GPU cluster.
- *Manpower.* The JRF is costed from month 3, because recruitment usually takes two months after sanction, and is upgraded to SRF after two years (month 27) as per norms. A Project Associate for the 12 recording months makes about three sessions a week, plus screening of up to 390 volunteers, feasible without stopping analysis. HRA is nil if hostel accommodation is provided. Fellowship rates follow the prevailing DST/ANRF norms and will be applied as notified.
- *Participant payments* cover 150 participants, the 10-session protocol pilot and 15 safeguard sessions (up to 55 recruited per stratum if the month-10 re-check needs them).
- *Prices* are estimates from list prices and Indian retail; written quotations will replace them before submission.

# 9. Use of outcomes, ethics and risks

## 9.1 Who uses the outcomes

| Output | Who uses it | For what |
|------------|------------|----------------|
| Reference error tables by skin tone, light, device and bitrate | Telehealth platform developers, standards bodies, regulators | Deciding where camera vital signs can be shown, and to whom, before any feature reaches patients |
| SAMA-150 dataset | Indian and international researchers, start-ups | Testing their own methods on Indian skin tones without collecting new data |
| SAMA method and toolkit | Developers of camera-based health apps | An open starting point that refuses readings it cannot trust and reports its reliability per group |
| Compression findings | Video-call and telemedicine engineers | Choosing between measuring on the phone and measuring from received video |

SAMA itself deploys nothing. A clinical project in patients, and the CDSCO software-as-a-medical-device route, would come after it and would need exactly this evidence. The work fits the IndiaAI Mission's Safe and Trusted AI pillar and the fairness principle of ICMR's 2023 ethical guidelines for AI in biomedical research and healthcare. Any licence will be non-exclusive, through SVNIT, with all academic outputs open.

## 9.2 Ethics and data protection

- **Approval.** Minimal-risk, non-invasive study. Recording starts only after approval from SVNIT's Institutional Ethics Committee or a DHR-registered committee, following the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017). [TO FILL: pilot approval reference and date; main-study application to be submitted on sanction.]
- **Consent and safety.** Written, tiered consent; anyone may stop at any time. Negative film clips come from the validated AFDI set and are mild; everyone is debriefed and given the contacts of the campus counsellor and Tele-MANAS (14416). The step test is offered only to those cleared by the PAR-Q+.
- **Data.** Raw video encrypted offline, access logged, never uploaded to a cloud; controlled access for faces, open release for derived signals; notice, consent, purpose limitation, retention and breach handling under the DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025.
- **Not a medical device.** SAMA makes no diagnosis; the interfaces are labelled for research only and never give participants readings as health information.

## 9.3 Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation | If it happens anyway |
|------------|--------|--------------------|----------------|
| The **lighter** stratum (ITA° > 28) fills slowly: about 15% of Indian adults in one colorimeter study | Medium–high | Screen about 330–390 volunteers with outreach for the lighter quota (pan-India campus, other Surat institutions); monthly quota tracking; pilot skin-tone distribution checked | H1 and H2 use continuous ITA°, so they stand; strata redefined by local tertiles before recruitment if the protocol pilot confirms the imbalance (pre-registered rule) |
| More spread, or a smaller effect, than assumed, so less power | Medium | 45 analysable per stratum; log endpoint for H1; protocol-pilot and month-10 re-check; up to 55 recruited per stratum budgeted | Effects reported with confidence intervals |
| Lossless video fills the storage | Medium | Face region-of-interest recording; about 20 TB planned on 4 × 18 TB drives (primary and encrypted backup) | Older sessions moved to the encrypted offline archive after QC |
| Compression removes most of the pulse at call bitrates | Medium | Ladder includes 2,000 and 1,000 kbps; measure-before-compress analysis | Strong finding in itself (prediction A or floor); remedy is on-device measurement |
| SAMA misses the H4 margin | Medium | Ablations show which step helps; the gate still reports reliability | Negative result published with the error budget, which is useful on its own |
| Ethics approval delayed | Medium | Pilot reviewed by the SVNIT IEC [TO FILL: reference]; main application filed on sanction; minimal-risk category | Set-up and synchronisation work continue; JRF costed from month 3 |
| JRF or Project Associate joins late | Medium | PI ran the pilot and the recorder is built; M.Tech projects support WP2 | Exploratory E1 dropped before any confirmatory work |
| Live-call recording unstable | Low–medium | Offline ladder is primary; live call only validates it | Ladder reported alone |
| Chosen phone lacks manual exposure control | Low | Model chosen after checking manual controls in Open Camera in the protocol pilot | Another model with verified controls |
| Privacy breach of face video | Low, high impact | Offline encryption, access log, no cloud | Breach protocol under the DPDP Rules |
| Another group publishes similar data | Medium | Measured skin tone, ECG, compression ladder and Indian sample together are distinct; preprint at month 20 | Results become complementary |
